slides.title: The workload
slides.subtitle: Three traces, re-cut per request on 2026-09-12: Claude Code (46,650 de-duplicated calls), Mooncake (39,632 requests), ServeGen (four Alibaba models).

slides.title: Three worlds, not one workload
slides.caption: Per-request input context (left) and output length (right), log scale; p10–p99 bar, p50 filled, p90 open, × max. Dashed lines: 29,184 tokens measured placed-region ceiling, and ≈103K whole-wafer total (derived, not measured). Claude Code: one user, 26,144 main-thread + 20,506 subagent calls, 2026-08-04 → 09-02. Mooncake output is hard-capped at 2,000. ServeGen publishes no p10.
slides.notes: Source: analyses/2026-09-12-trace-length-distributions/ (README, plot_length_distributions.py, results/lengths.json). Recomputed from the existing study files: gc-trace steps.csv, mooncake data/*.jsonl, servegen lengths.json. Per-turn Claude Code: decode p50 5.8K / p90 23.5K, new prefill p50 10.9K / p90 254K; per session max context p50 94K / p90 281K / p99 965K. ServeGen R1 reasoning share of output p50 76%; requests with output > 2K are 16% of requests but 57% of decode tokens.

slides.title: Only the agentic harness produces the case where not even one request fits
items: Claude Code: huge input (p50 100–300K), medium output (a few K to ~20K per turn)
Mooncake: input a few K, output a few hundred — p99 input 62–85K
ServeGen R1: input a few hundred, output a few thousand — p99 input ≤ 23K
Every non-agentic trace has p99 input inside the measured 29,184-token ceiling
The whole-wafer total (≈103K, derived) holds tens of such sessions — and a fraction of one Claude Code request
So 'grow one request' vs 'park many requests' has no workload-independent answer
slides.notes: 4b-pp-demo's conclusion for the on-chip KV debate. The 103K figure is 29K placed + ≈74K unplaced SRAM, derived not measured. Supporting measured numbers from the 09-03/09-05 captures (not new): 99% of Claude Code calls have a successor re-reading ≥95% of their KV within 10–18 s; not keeping it costs a median 13.9 s reload = 61% of the next call's latency; decode-stream concurrency p50 = 1 in both traces.

Main-thread output is 11.6% of that class's token traffic; subagents 1.5%
Correction to last week: the 'median context 309K' was the main-thread number
Including subagent calls, the per-call median is 197K — the figure used from here on

slides.title: The GPU baseline
slides.subtitle: SGLang 0.5.19 on one H100 80GB, vanilla, every cell measured. Same model on both sides for the first time.

slides.title: The wafer leads single-stream decode by 4–5× and trails prefill by 7×
slides.subtitle: Qwen3-4B. CS-3 rates as reported by the source session (750 MHz); clock convention pending.
slides.notes: Source: docs/reports/2026-09-13-sglang-qwen3-4b-h100-baseline.md and 4b-wide-layer Round 156. CS-3 column: decode cycles/step = 681K + 16.1 × context, converted at 750 MHz by the source session. At 0.85 GHz the CS-3 rates rise by 1.133 and the leads become ~5.4× / 4.5× / 2.6× shallower; the batched and prefill deficits shrink to ~2.0× and ~6×. Le to decide which clock the deck uses. Finding 10 (prefill behind) goes from extrapolated to measured.

slides.title: Our only measured advantage applies exclusively to the workload we cannot hold
items: Confirmed: prefill is ~7× behind — finding 10 is now measured, not extrapolated
Killed: the 'fast recompute engine for short-context multi-tenant traffic' claim
Even the analytical thin-stage forced prefill (31–43K tok/s) is 1.6–2.2× slower than the H100's measured native prefill
There is no prefill-side wedge anywhere on the roadmap
Median agentic turn at short context: CS-3 6.9 s vs H100 28 s
At the real 197K context: H100 ~75 s, CS-3 cannot hold it at all
slides.notes: 4b-wide-layer Round 156. The single-stream decode lead (4.0–4.7×) grows with context — and the workload with long context is the one that does not fit.

slides.title: The capacity case
slides.subtitle: Every rung of the on-chip ladder against the traces, then the two ways around it: more wafers, or a link.

slides.eyebrow: Capacity · the ladder against the traces
slides.title: No rung reaches the agent harness; the workloads it reaches also fit in 80 GB of HBM
slides.subtitle: Ceilings are analytical except today's, which is measured. Trace percentiles: Claude Code p50 197K, Mooncake p99 85K, ServeGen p99 23K.
slides.notes: 4b-wide-layer Rounds 153–154. The far pool at 167K is the score-buffer wall, not a storage limit: fp8 storage alone allows ≈225K, and chunked scoring (lever C3, owned by the 4b-chunked-softmax session) removes the wall. The yes/no columns compare each ceiling against the quoted trace percentile; they are my reading of the numbers the session gave, not a table the session produced.

slides.title: Capacity cannot reach the workload that wants it; the workloads it reaches do not need it.
slides.subtitle: The reopener is the score-buffer wall: fp8 storage plus chunked scoring would clear the 197K median for ~55% of agent calls — all derived.
slides.notes: 4b-wide-layer Round 153. The sentence is the session's; the reopener is Round 154's.

slides.title: Multi-card does not rescue capacity: it halves the one thing we lead
items: Measured: 175 µs per wafer per token at today's layout
29K → 197K needs ≈ 6 extra wafers, i.e. +1.01 ms per token (derived)
Decode goes from 1.05 to 2.06 ms per token: 954 → 485 tok/s
A negative-sum trade in the one dimension where the wafer is ahead
slides.notes: 4b-wide-layer Round 156/157. The 175 µs is measured; the extension is arithmetic. tok/s at 750 MHz as reported.

slides.title: Per token, attention reads the whole KV — it cannot cross a link
slides.subtitle: Card-to-card interconnect at 1.2 Tbit/s (150 GB/s), per Le; not measured in this project. Whole decode step on the wafer is 1.0 ms.
slides.notes: 4b-wide-layer Round 159. Fitting 29K of KV into half a token budget needs ≈8 TB/s — the link is 53× short — and the H100 reads the same KV 22× faster from HBM. This is a bandwidth-class fact, not an engineering gap. The earlier 171 µs crossing figure was the public API and is retracted (see Corrections).

slides.eyebrow: Capacity · what the link does buy
slides.title: KV must live where the attention compute is; the link carries activations, and AFD is a weights-side solution
items: Activations: 5 KB per layer, 34 ns of wire — pure latency
36 layers × 6–10 µs round trip = 0.22–0.36 ms per token: affordable
So attention–FFN disaggregation is viable on the real interconnect
But it removes FFN weight traffic: worth 57.3% at 4K, only 15.0% at 197K
A dense 4B on an 80 GB GPU is AFD's worst case — which is why NVIDIA keeps attention + KV together
slides.notes: 4b-wide-layer Round 159. The 6–10 µs round trip is Le's interconnect figure plus turnaround, unmeasured here. AFD = Attention–FFN Disaggregation, NVIDIA's split in which the GPU holds prefill and decode attention plus the whole KV and the LPX side does FFN/MoE.

slides.title: The prefix × decode spectrum
slides.subtitle: Four configurations across eleven workload scenarios, derived from each machine's measured rates. Per-request wall time.

slides.title: PD-split wins every scenario that fits: the GPU prefills, the wafer decodes
slides.subtitle: ms per request. PD-split = GPU prefill → link → CS-3 decode. Derived from measured rates; link at 0.98 µs per prefix token (unmeasured).
slides.notes: 4b-wide-layer Round 171. Modelling: CS-3 decode = (681K + 16.1·C) cycles at 750 MHz; H100 decode = 4.60 + 0.0489·C/1K ms (fit to measured 1K–32K); H100 prefill measured, held at the 32K rate beyond 32K (optimistic for H100). GPU-streamed = KV stays on the GPU and the whole cache crosses per token. PD-split's decode side is the wafer, so it keeps the 29K ceiling. Best in every row here is PD-split.

slides.title: The longer the prefix, the more the 7× prefill deficit costs CS-3 alone
slides.subtitle: ms per request. Same model as the previous slide.
slides.notes: 4b-wide-layer Round 171. PD-split's margin over CS-3 alone: 1.03× at 208 tokens, 1.5× at 2.4K, 2.3× at 6.9K, 2.4× at 17K, 3.9× at 27K. Its weakest win is long-prefix/tiny-decode (classification), where the H100 alone is within 8%.

slides.title: Above 29K only the H100 serves — PD-split does not extend the ceiling, because its decode side is the wafer
slides.subtitle: ms per request. The Claude Code row is a frontier-model workload a 4B never serves; it is here for completeness, not as a target.
slides.notes: 4b-wide-layer Round 171 and Round 168. H100 prefill beyond 32K is held at the 32K rate, so these two H100 times are understated. The GPU-streamed column is worse than the H100 alone in every row of the spectrum except the 680-token one, and 8–13× worse above 29K: 'keep KV on the GPU' is dead at every scale.

slides.title: Prefix length sets the margin over CS-3 alone; decode share sets the margin over the H100
items: Over CS-3 alone: 1.03× at a 208-token prefix, rising to 3.9× at 27K — PD-split is the prefill fix
Over H100 alone: 5.0× where decode is ~100% of the work, down to 1.08× at 4% — the decode advantage
The 29K wall decides participation; above it the GPU is alone, with or without a wafer
Short-prefix / long-decode (reasoning) is the wafer's home turf: 5× over H100 alone, PD-split barely needed
Long-prefix / short-decode (RAG, summarisation) needs PD-split, and the H100 is competitive
PD-split was ruled out earlier on a 3.2 GB/s H2D measurement; the real link is 62–176× that requirement
slides.notes: 4b-wide-layer Rounds 169 and 171. The 3.2 GB/s was host-to-wafer memcpy through the public API, a different leg from the card-to-card interconnect.

slides.title: The same 167K holds zero agentic requests or 803 ServeGen requests
slides.subtitle: Capacity spent on one request's depth, or on many requests' prefixes. Derived.
slides.notes: 4b-wide-layer Round 164. The frontier is two-dimensional and only the depth axis has been pushed.

slides.title: Push breadth first: prefix reuse inside today's 29K, with harvesting as the mechanism
items: Prefix reuse is startable inside today's 29K, with two independent justifications
Our prefill is 7× slower, so avoiding a re-prefill is worth 7× more to us: 10.9K tokens cost the H100 156 ms and CS-3 1,147 ms
ServeGen traffic is 3.9 : 1 prefill-to-decode by token
Near-pool harvesting is the one rung already priced: 1.17 cycles per word, inside the ≤ 2 gate (simfab microbench)
Then the depth-vs-breadth allocation curve
Do not chase 167K or 225K as a target
slides.notes: 4b-wide-layer Round 164. The 1.17 cyc/word figure came from the fused-block thread's simfab microbench, which also corrected a 13 cyc/word relay artefact. Two measurements still missing: the width axis (four measured points on height, none on width), and the wafer-edge round trip to a GPU (waits on Cerebras opening the API).

slides.title: Layout C
slides.subtitle: One decoder layer cut into three thin stages on a single 256×256 block. Implemented through a five-layer group, measured on CS-3, closed on 2026-09-13.

slides.title: Eight groups of five layers on a 650 × 1028 footprint, with head and tail on the left
slides.caption: Wafer map only; the colour ledger is in the source figure. Analytical placement from a design and source audit, not a compiled full model.
slides.notes: Source: docs/diagrams/2026-09-13-layoutC-color-regions.png (.excalidraw editable). Northbound groups G4–G7 are mirrored proposals with no chip-fit, route, queue or SRAM validation. Purple columns are router-only activation bridges; orange x=645 is the KV feeder reservation.

slides.title: A1 and A3 share the left half; A2 takes the whole right half
slides.caption: Compiled miniature (16 × 16 core, one layer, simulator validation) with the same shape as the full geometry: A1 128 × 80 (32 hidden per row), spare 128 × 16, A3 128 × 160 (16 per row), A2 128 × 256 (10 per row). 65,536 PEs reserved, 63,488 active.
slides.notes: Source: docs/diagrams/2026-09-10-layoutC-tall-a2.png; geometry source of truth is docs/reports/2026-09-13-layoutC-implementation-handoff.md §3. Why the row shards are 32/10/16 and which tensor axis each stage shards: the hidden-reshard and weight-axes figures in the appendix.

slides.title: 3.7–3.9× the original's single-layer latency in half the PEs
slides.subtitle: Raw CS-3 device cycles, batch 1, BF16, one layer. Serialized latency, not pipelined throughput; synthetic weights.
columns: Layout C A1 + A2 + A3 (65,536 PE)
slides.notes: Source: docs/reports/2026-09-13-layoutC-single-layer-performance.md (+ evidence JSON). Three independent jobs per cell, 33 tokens each, first 4 dropped, median of 29 then median across jobs. All 1,013,760 output elements exact against each geometry's own operation-order oracle. Common boundary: START enqueue → all output rows complete on one collector PE; empty cost 8,231 cycles, not subtracted. Context sensitivity is tiny on both sides: +0.42 / +0.47 cycles per KV position. The bar chart is in the appendix.

slides.title: FLOP does not predict time here: FFN has 2× the MACs, ATTN takes 2× the time
slides.caption: The original ATTN and FFN blocks on three axes. TIME is 4b-wide-layer's phase-TSC profile (per layer per token, 2K, full 256 × 256 square); FLOP is derived MACs per PE; SRAM is the compiled per-PE total. ATTN also grows with context (T_attn / T_ffn → ~2.7 at 8K); FFN is flat.
slides.notes: Source: docs/reports/2026-09-13-attn-vs-ffn-three-axes.png (footnote cropped for the slide; the FLOP-panel subtitle still collides with the 1200 tick — re-export pending). Numbers: ATTN 560 MACs / 11,886 cycles / 31.75 KB; FFN 1,140 MACs / 5,802 cycles / 29.77 KB. SRAM from demo/qwen3-4b-thin-stage/results/cs3/out_S1B_2K/msize.txt. This replaces the per-PE-work bar chart, which plotted FLOP only and is withdrawn (Corrections).

slides.eyebrow: Layout C · the explanation that survived
slides.title: The kernel is comm- and latency-bound, so a three-way cut pays three coordination costs
items: The MAC model that named A3 (FFN) as the pacing stage predicted the ratio and got the mechanism backwards — withdrawn
Measured: ATTN paces the original at 2.05× FFN's time, and FFN idles
Per-stage time for A1 / A2 / A3 was never measured; only the combined single-layer numbers exist
Separately measured: ATTN and FFN as independent pipelined stages give 1.47× at 2K and 1.40× at 8K
That result keeps two blocks and overlaps them — the lever layout C gave up
slides.notes: 4b-mini-ppl-debug's correction plus docs/reports/2026-09-13-layoutC-performance-conclusion.md §5b. Also withdrawn with the MAC model: the '2.65× optimal three-way split' floor and the 0.31× / 0.62× first-order pipelined-throughput figures.

slides.title: The first five-layer group with on-wafer feedback runs on CS-3, exact
items: Mini geometry: 5 layers × 33 tokens, 10,560 output elements exact
Full geometry: 5 layers × 2 tokens, 5,120 exact
Full cache probe: 83,886,080 K/V values and every cursor pass; a one-bit-flip negative control fails as it should
Router-only strip transport with the marker / ACK / reset / START protocol validated both directions, with dropped- and duplicated-fragment controls
Two device defects found and fixed on 09-10: A2 RoPE reset overwriting XKCache; cut-chain zero local-layer count
slides.notes: Sources: docs/reports/2026-09-13-layoutC-first-group-feedback.md, docs/reports/2026-09-10-layoutC-kv-fix.md. The transport, checker and handoff work carry over to the fused block.

slides.title: Closed. Next: one fused 256 × 256 block with attention state on one PE in N
items: The two-group D17 link is paused (Le, 09-13)
Fused block: FFN + QKV on every PE; attention heavy state on 1-in-N PEs; the rest hold KV and a minimal scan
Gate: compile-only SRAM of the three PE images
First-order expectation: ~1.0× the original's latency in half the area — derived, not measured
Layout C's structural cause — three serial stages sharing one block's area — does not apply to a fused block
slides.notes: 4b-mini-ppl-debug relaying Le's 09-13 decision. Memory note (layoutc-closed-fused-sparse-attention-next) adds: fusion 1.34× at fixed wafer and SRAM-ahead vs the FFN block; gate = compile-only .text-vs-layer-halving; streaming measured cheap. Those figures were not in the message sent to this deck and are not on the slide.

slides.title: Why the hardware advantage does not come out
slides.subtitle: A property of this kernel, not of the architecture — the scoping caveat is on the slide.

slides.title: 87% of per-layer time is independent of how much work each PE does
items: Least-squares on the measured height ladder: T = 10,398 + 855 × W (W = per-PE work) — halving the area moved time by 1.4%
Per PE per layer: 3,080 bytes in ~17,688 cycles = 0.174 B/cycle against ~27 available, 0.63% utilisation
Mechanism: 10 hidden + 16 attention values per PE, so a QKV matvec is 160 MACs against ~100 cycles of DSD setup; 8–9.6K of the fixed term is collectives
Aggregate: 6,269× the bandwidth converted into 4.7×; 0.045% utilisation against the H100's 59.7%
Scope: Cerebras quotes CS-5 at 10,000 tok/s per user on 31B–120B models — a model 8–30× larger running 10× faster. These are this kernel's numbers, not the architecture's
Their own rates back-solve to 0.24–1.52% of aggregate bandwidth, so the diagnosis (latency-bound) is corroborated; the lever it implies is speculative decoding, not yet pulled
slides.notes: 4b-wide-layer Rounds 158 and 162. Speculative decoding amortises the fixed term and the KV scan; batching amortises only the first, and our batching measured 2.2×. Unaffected by the caveat: everything trace-based — the three workload shapes, AFD's weights-side nature, MoE sparsity inverting sign, KV not crossing a link.

slides.title: Industry context and positioning
slides.subtitle: What NVIDIA's LPX and Cerebras's CS-6 say about the boundary, and how to frame the argument.

slides.title: Both LPX and CS-6 add a DRAM tier; the field is moving from total residency to tiering
items: NVIDIA Groq 3 LPX: 500 MB compiler-managed SRAM per chip, 128 GB rack-wide, 96 C2C links = 2.5 TB/s per chip, plus 256 GB + 128 GB DRAM
LPX does FFN / MoE; the GPUs hold prefill and decode attention and the whole KV — attention–FFN disaggregation with compile-time static allocation
Shared design constant: a full SRAM sweep is ~3.3 µs on LPX and ~2.1 µs on WSE-3
The difference is the boundary: LPX made the chip edge part of the compiler's schedule; Cerebras has no edge inside a wafer
Cerebras CS-6 (Hot Chips 2026) adds 3D-stacked DRAM — the tier CS-3 lacks. Roadmap, no capacity or bandwidth numbers published
If KV moved there the thresholds are 4.0 TB/s at 29K, 27.1 TB/s at 197K (8.1× HBM), 84.6 TB/s at p90 — derived
slides.notes: 4b-wide-layer Rounds 158 and 162, from the NVIDIA blog and the Cerebras Hot Chips 2026 post. LPX also uses a plesiosynchronous protocol aligning hundreds of chips as one system.

points: Numbers are this kernel's, not the architecture's

slides.eyebrow: Positioning · the residency frontier in three layers
slides.title: Taxonomy is AFD's table; placement is the measured, novel part; method is what survived this week
items: Taxonomy: dense weights tierable; MoE experts must be tiered; KV not tierable (53× short); activations trivially tierable
Placement: inside the resident tier, per-PE distribution binds, not aggregate capacity — halving width halves the ceiling, fusion doubles it, at identical totals
Per-PE footprint is not weight-dominated: 24.8 of the ATTN block's 31.8 KB is code, buffers and KV machinery
Method: across ~12 contested claims this week, the single predictor of survival was whether the measurement carried a control; the failure mode recurred twelve times
CS-3 is the extremal no-tier point, so every residency decision is forced into the open and measurable
